sql-select: A shop keeps its data in a database. SQL is the language you use to ask that database questions, such as "what do we sell, and at what price?". This first lesson teaches the one statement every question starts with: SELECT. ### Tables, rows and columns A table is a grid of data, like one sheet of a spreadsheet. Each row is one thing (one customer, one product). Each column is one piece of information about that thing (a name, a price). Every column has a name, and every row has a value in each column. Our sample shop has five tables: customers (10 people), products (12 items for sale), orders (15 orders), order_items (which products went into which order) and employees (8 staff). A query is a question written in SQL. When you run it, the database answers with a result: a new, temporary table. The page shows that result under each example. ### SELECT and FROM: show everything ~~~sql SELECT * FROM products; ~~~ - SELECT: "show me these columns". It is always the first word of a question. - *: the star is a shortcut for "every column", in the order the table stores them. - FROM products: the table to read. Without FROM, the database would not know where to look. - ;: the semicolon marks the end of one statement, like a full stop ends a sentence. The result has 12 rows, one per product, and 5 columns: id, name, category, price and stock. The id column is a unique number that identifies each row. ### Picking only some columns Usually you do not want every column. List the ones you need, separated by commas. ~~~sql SELECT name, price FROM products; ~~~ - SELECT name, price: keep only these two columns, in this order. - FROM products: still read every row of the products table. You still get 12 rows, because you did not ask to drop any row. You only get 2 columns now. The order of the names after SELECT decides the order of the columns in the result. ### Reading another table The same pattern works on any table. Only the table name and the column names change. ~~~sql SELECT name, email FROM customers; ~~~ - SELECT name, email: two columns that exist in the customers table. - FROM customers: read the customers table instead of products. The result has 10 rows, one per customer, from Alice Martin to Jules Petit. If you ask for a column that does not exist in that table, you get an error such as "no such column". ### Calculating a new column with AS A column in SELECT can be a calculation. The database computes it for every row. ~~~sql SELECT name, price, price * 1.2 AS price_with_tax FROM products; ~~~ - price * 1.2: multiply each price by 1.2. The symbols + - * / work like on a calculator. Here * means "times", not "every column". - AS price_with_tax: give the new column a readable name, called an alias. Without AS, the column would be titled with the formula itself. - FROM products: still 12 rows. The Laptop Pro 14 costs 1299, so its price_with_tax shows 1558.8. The calculation only exists in the result. The products table itself is not changed. Some values come out with long tails, such as 35.879999999999995 for the Wireless Mouse. That is a normal side effect of how computers store decimals; a later lesson shows how to round them. ### Writing style SQL keywords are not case sensitive: select and SELECT do the same thing. Writing keywords in capitals and names in lower case makes queries easier to read. You can split a query over several lines; line breaks and extra spaces do not matter. Two dashes -- start a comment: everything after them on that line is ignored by the database. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the comma between column names. SELECT name city is read as "column name, renamed to city", which is not what you meant. - Misspelling a column or table name. Look at the table shown on the page to check the exact spelling. - Putting FROM before SELECT. The order is always SELECT first, then FROM. ### Recap - A table is made of rows (things) and columns (facts about them). A query returns a result table. - SELECT columns FROM table; lists the columns you want from a table. - * means every column; a comma separated list picks specific ones. - AS names a column in the result, including calculated ones.
sql-where: Most real questions are about some rows, not all of them: "which products are expensive?" or "which books cost 40 or less?". WHERE lets you keep only the rows that match a condition. ### WHERE with a number comparison ~~~sql SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > 100; ~~~ - FROM products: start with all 12 products. - WHERE price > 100: test each row. Rows where the condition is true are kept, the others are dropped. - SELECT name, price: from the rows that survived, show these two columns. The result has 4 rows: Laptop Pro 14, Noise-Cancelling Headphones, Standing Desk and Ergonomic Chair. Notice the order in which the database works: it reads the table (FROM), then filters rows (WHERE), and only then picks the columns (SELECT). That is why you can filter on a column you do not display. The comparison operators are: - = equal to, and <> not equal to (!= also works) - < less than, and <= less than or equal to - > greater than, and >= greater than or equal to ### Text values need quotes ~~~sql SELECT name, category FROM products WHERE category <> 'Electronics'; ~~~ - WHERE category <> 'Electronics': keep rows whose category is anything other than Electronics. - 'Electronics': text values go between single quotes. Without quotes, SQL would look for a column called Electronics. The result has 8 rows: the 3 Furniture, 3 Books and 2 Grocery products. Text comparison with = is exact, so 'electronics' in lower case would not match 'Electronics'. Numbers are written without quotes. ### AND: both conditions must be true ~~~sql SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE category = 'Books' AND price <= 40; ~~~ - category = 'Books': first test. - AND price <= 40: second test. A row is kept only when both tests are true. The result has 2 rows: Python Crash Course (35) and Clean Code (38.5). SQL Cookbook is a book too, but it costs 45, so it fails the second test. You can chain as many AND conditions as you like. ### OR and NOT OR keeps a row when at least one condition is true. NOT flips a condition: true becomes false. ~~~sql SELECT name, category FROM products WHERE category = 'Books' OR category = 'Grocery'; ~~~ - category = 'Books' OR category = 'Grocery': a row passes if it is a book, or a grocery item. The result has 5 rows: the 3 books and the 2 grocery items. Writing WHERE NOT category = 'Books' would instead return the 9 products that are not books. ### Parentheses when mixing AND and OR AND is evaluated before OR, just like multiplication comes before addition. Use parentheses to say exactly what you mean. ~~~sql SELECT name, category, price FROM products WHERE (category = 'Books' OR category = 'Grocery') AND price < 20; ~~~ - (category = 'Books' OR category = 'Grocery'): this part is worked out first, giving the 5 books and grocery items. - AND price < 20: of those, keep the ones under 20. The result has 2 rows: Coffee Beans 1kg (18.9) and Green Tea Box (9.5). Without the parentheses, SQL would read it as "books, or grocery items under 20", and all 3 books would come back too. ### Common mistakes - Using double quotes or no quotes for text: write 'Books', with single quotes. - Writing category = 'Books' OR 'Grocery'. Each side of OR must be a full condition: category = 'Books' OR category = 'Grocery'. - Mixing AND and OR without parentheses and getting extra rows. - Putting WHERE before FROM. The order is SELECT, FROM, WHERE. ### Recap - WHERE condition keeps only the rows where the condition is true. - The database runs FROM first, then WHERE, then SELECT. - Compare with = <> < <= > >=; text goes in single quotes. - AND needs both conditions, OR needs at least one, NOT reverses one. Use parentheses when you mix them.
sql-order: A list is far more useful when it is sorted: cheapest products first, newest orders on top, or just the top few. This lesson covers sorting with ORDER BY, cutting the list with LIMIT, and removing duplicates with DISTINCT. ### ORDER BY: sort the result Without ORDER BY, rows come back in whatever order the database finds convenient. That order is not guaranteed, so never rely on it. ~~~sql SELECT name, stock FROM products ORDER BY stock; ~~~ - FROM products: all 12 products. - SELECT name, stock: two columns. - ORDER BY stock: sort the rows by the stock column, smallest value first. The result starts with Standing Desk (8 in stock) and ends with Green Tea Box (200). Text columns sort alphabetically, and dates written as 'YYYY-MM-DD' sort from oldest to newest. ### ASC and DESC: choose the direction ASC means ascending (smallest first) and is the default, so you rarely write it. DESC means descending: largest first. ~~~sql SELECT name, stock FROM products ORDER BY stock DESC; ~~~ - ORDER BY stock DESC: sort by stock, largest first. Now Green Tea Box (200) comes first and Standing Desk (8) comes last. DESC applies only to the column written right before it. ### Sorting by several columns ~~~sql SELECT category, name, price FROM products ORDER BY category, price DESC; ~~~ - ORDER BY category: first sort by category, alphabetically (Books, Electronics, Furniture, Grocery). - , price DESC: when two rows have the same category, sort them by price, highest first. The 12 rows come back grouped: the 3 Books with SQL Cookbook (45) first, then the 4 Electronics with Laptop Pro 14 (1299) first, and so on. The second column only matters to break ties in the first. ### LIMIT: keep only the first rows ~~~sql SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price LIMIT 3; ~~~ - ORDER BY price: sort from cheapest to most expensive. - LIMIT 3: after sorting, keep only the first 3 rows. The result is Green Tea Box (9.5), Coffee Beans 1kg (18.9) and Wireless Mouse (29.9): the 3 cheapest products. LIMIT goes at the very end of the query. Without ORDER BY, LIMIT 3 would give you 3 rows, but not necessarily the right ones. This is the order in which the database works through a query so far: FROM (read the table), WHERE (filter rows), SELECT (pick and calculate columns), ORDER BY (sort), LIMIT (cut). Because SELECT runs before ORDER BY, you can sort by an alias you created with AS. ### DISTINCT: each value only once ~~~sql SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers; ~~~ - SELECT DISTINCT city: show the city column, but remove duplicate rows from the result. - FROM customers: the 10 customers. The 10 customers live in only a few places, so the result has 6 rows: Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, Nantes and an empty value. That empty value is NULL, meaning "unknown": one customer has no city. You will meet NULL properly in the next lesson. DISTINCT applies to the whole row: SELECT DISTINCT category, name would remove only rows where both values repeat. ### Common mistakes - Expecting a sorted result without ORDER BY. - Writing LIMIT before ORDER BY. The order is always ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT ... - Thinking DESC applies to every sort column. In ORDER BY category, price DESC only price is descending. - Using LIMIT to find "the top N" without sorting first in the right direction. ### Recap - ORDER BY column sorts the result; ASC (default) is smallest first, DESC is largest first. - Several sort columns are separated by commas; later ones break ties. - LIMIT n keeps the first n rows after sorting. - DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result. - Evaluation order: FROM, WHERE, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
sql-in: Marketing asks: "which customers live in Paris or Bordeaux?", "which products cost between 30 and 50?", "which customers have no city on file?". You could write these with AND and OR, but SQL has shorter, clearer tools: IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and IS NULL. ### IN: one of a list ~~~sql SELECT name, city FROM customers WHERE city IN ('Paris', 'Bordeaux'); ~~~ - FROM customers: the 10 customers. - WHERE city IN ('Paris', 'Bordeaux'): keep a row if its city equals any value in the list. The list goes in parentheses, values separated by commas. - SELECT name, city: show who they are and where they live. The result has 4 rows: Alice Martin, Chloe Dubois and Hugo Bernard (Paris), and Grace Lee (Bordeaux). It means exactly the same as city = 'Paris' OR city = 'Bordeaux', but stays short even with ten values. NOT IN (...) keeps rows that match none of the values. ### BETWEEN: a range, both ends included ~~~sql SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 30 AND 50; ~~~ - WHERE price BETWEEN 30 AND 50: keep prices from 30 up to 50. Both ends count, so a price of exactly 30 or exactly 50 would be kept. The result has 5 rows: USB-C Hub (49), Desk Lamp (39.9), Python Crash Course (35), SQL Cookbook (45) and Clean Code (38.5). It is the same as price >= 30 AND price <= 50. Always write the smaller value first. ### BETWEEN on dates In this database, dates are stored as text in the form 'YYYY-MM-DD' (year, month, day). Because the biggest unit comes first, sorting or comparing this text gives the same answer as comparing real dates. So BETWEEN works on them, as long as you put the dates in quotes. ~~~sql SELECT id, customer_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31'; ~~~ - WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31': keep orders placed in March 2025, the first and last day included. The result has 4 rows: orders 7, 8, 9 and 10. Writing the date without quotes, like 2025-03-01, would be read as a subtraction (2025 minus 3 minus 1). ### LIKE: text patterns with % and _ LIKE compares text to a pattern. Two symbols act as wildcards: - % stands for any number of characters, including none. - _ (underscore) stands for exactly one character. ~~~sql SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%desk%'; ~~~ - '%desk%': anything, then "desk", then anything. In other words, "contains desk". The result has 2 rows: Standing Desk and Desk Lamp. In SQLite, LIKE ignores upper and lower case for plain letters, which is why "desk" matched "Desk". Other patterns: 'C%' means "starts with C" (Clean Code, Coffee Beans 1kg) and '%@mail.com' means "ends with @mail.com". ~~~sql SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '_o%'; ~~~ - '_o%': exactly one character, then the letter o, then anything. So "the second letter is o". The result has 2 rows: Noise-Cancelling Headphones and Coffee Beans 1kg. ### NULL: a missing value NULL means "no value, unknown". It is not zero and not an empty text. Farid Haddad has no city, so his city is NULL. Because NULL is unknown, any comparison with it, even city = NULL, is never true. To test for it you must use the special operators IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. ~~~sql SELECT name, city FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL; ~~~ - WHERE city IS NULL: keep rows where city has no value. The result has 1 row: Farid Haddad, with an empty city. With IS NOT NULL you would get the other 9 customers. ### Combining them All of these are just conditions, so you can join them with AND and OR like any other test: for example WHERE category IN ('Books', 'Grocery') AND price BETWEEN 10 AND 40 keeps books and grocery items priced 10 to 40. ### Common mistakes - Writing city = NULL. It never matches; use city IS NULL. - Forgetting the quotes around dates or around values inside IN. - Using LIKE without a wildcard: LIKE 'Desk' only matches the exact text Desk. - Expecting BETWEEN to exclude its end points. Both ends are included. ### Recap - IN (a, b, c): the value is one of a list. - BETWEEN low AND high: inside a range, ends included; works on numbers and on 'YYYY-MM-DD' dates. - LIKE with % (any characters) and _ (one character) matches text patterns. - NULL is a missing value; test it with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
sql-case: Reports often need labels that are not stored in the table: "is this stock level low or fine?", "is this order still open?". CASE lets you build such a label row by row, and COALESCE fills in missing values. ### CASE: if, then, else CASE is SQL's way of saying "if this, then that, otherwise something else". It goes in the SELECT list and produces a new, calculated column. ~~~sql SELECT name, stock, CASE WHEN stock >= 100 THEN 'plenty' WHEN stock >= 20 THEN 'ok' ELSE 'low' END AS stock_level FROM products; ~~~ - FROM products: the 12 products. - CASE: starts the decision. - WHEN stock >= 100 THEN 'plenty': if the condition is true, the value is 'plenty'. - WHEN stock >= 20 THEN 'ok': checked only for rows that did not match the first WHEN. - ELSE 'low': the value when no WHEN matched. - END: closes the CASE. It is required. - AS stock_level: names the new column. The result has 12 rows. Wireless Mouse (150), Coffee Beans 1kg (100) and Green Tea Box (200) are 'plenty'. Standing Desk (8), Laptop Pro 14 (12) and Ergonomic Chair (15) are 'low'. The other 6 are 'ok'. ### Order of the WHEN lines matters The database tests the WHEN lines from top to bottom and stops at the first one that is true. Green Tea Box has 200 in stock, which is also >= 20, but it never reaches the second line because the first already matched. If you wrote the >= 20 line first, every product with 100 or more would wrongly be labelled 'ok'. So with "at least" thresholds, put the biggest threshold first. ### CASE on text values ~~~sql SELECT id, status, CASE WHEN status IN ('pending', 'shipped') THEN 'open' ELSE 'closed' END AS state FROM orders; ~~~ - WHEN status IN ('pending', 'shipped'): any condition you can write in WHERE also works in a WHEN, including IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and AND. - ELSE 'closed': delivered and cancelled orders. The result has 15 rows. Orders 7, 10 and 12 are 'open'; the other 12 are 'closed'. ### No ELSE means NULL ~~~sql SELECT name, price, CASE WHEN price > 300 THEN 'big ticket' END AS note FROM products; ~~~ - CASE WHEN price > 300 THEN 'big ticket' END: there is no ELSE line. Laptop Pro 14, Standing Desk and Ergonomic Chair get 'big ticket'. The other 9 rows get NULL, shown as an empty cell, because nothing matched and there was no ELSE to fall back on. ### COALESCE: the first value that is not NULL COALESCE(a, b, ...) looks at its values from left to right and returns the first one that is not NULL. It is the quickest way to show a default instead of an empty cell. ~~~sql SELECT name, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city FROM customers; ~~~ - COALESCE(city, 'Unknown'): if city has a value, use it; if it is NULL, use 'Unknown'. - AS city: keep the familiar column name. The result has 10 rows. Farid Haddad, whose city is NULL, now shows 'Unknown'. Everyone else shows their real city. The table itself is not changed; only the result is. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting END, which gives a syntax error. - Putting the thresholds in the wrong order, so a smaller test catches rows first. - Forgetting the comma before CASE in the SELECT list. - Forgetting AS name, which leaves the whole CASE text as the column title. ### Recap - CASE WHEN condition THEN value ... ELSE value END creates a calculated column, row by row. - WHEN lines are tested top to bottom; the first true one wins. - Without ELSE, rows that match nothing get NULL. - COALESCE(a, b) returns the first value that is not NULL, ideal for defaults.
sql-agg: Managers rarely want a list of every row. They want one number: "how many orders do we have?", "how many items are in stock?", "what is the cheapest product?". Aggregate functions answer that kind of question: they read many rows and squash them into a single value. ### COUNT: how many rows ~~~sql SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; ~~~ - FROM orders: the 15 orders. - COUNT(*): count the rows. The * inside the parentheses means "whole rows", whatever their content. The result is a single row with a single value: 15. A function is a named operation that takes values between parentheses and gives back a result. COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX are the five classic aggregate functions. ### COUNT(column) and COUNT(DISTINCT column) ~~~sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers, COUNT(city) AS with_city, COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS cities FROM customers; ~~~ - COUNT(*) AS customers: all 10 rows. - COUNT(city) AS with_city: counts only the rows where city is not NULL. Farid Haddad has no city, so this gives 9. - COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS cities: counts the different non-NULL values. Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux and Nantes give 5. - AS: names each result column, as usual. One row comes back: 10, 9, 5. Several aggregates can sit side by side in the same SELECT, separated by commas. ### SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX ~~~sql SELECT SUM(stock) AS total_units, AVG(stock) AS avg_units, MIN(stock) AS lowest, MAX(stock) AS highest FROM products; ~~~ - SUM(stock): adds up the stock of all 12 products: 755 units. - AVG(stock): the average, which is the sum divided by the number of values: 62.916666666666664. - MIN(stock): the smallest value, 8 (the Standing Desk). - MAX(stock): the largest value, 200 (the Green Tea Box). All four functions ignore NULL values. MIN and MAX also work on text and on dates: MIN(order_date) on the orders table gives the first order date, '2025-01-05'. ### ROUND: tidy decimals The average above has far too many decimals. ROUND(value, digits) rounds a number to the given number of decimal places. You can put one function inside another: the inner one is worked out first. ~~~sql SELECT ROUND(AVG(stock), 2) AS avg_units, ROUND(AVG(stock)) AS avg_whole FROM products; ~~~ - AVG(stock): first, compute the average, 62.9166... - ROUND(..., 2): then round it to 2 decimals: 62.92. - ROUND(...): without the second number, it rounds to a whole number: 63.0. ### Aggregates after WHERE WHERE runs before the aggregate functions. So you can first choose which rows to include, then summarise them. ~~~sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS products, SUM(stock) AS units, MIN(name) AS first_name FROM products WHERE category = 'Electronics'; ~~~ - FROM products: 12 rows. - WHERE category = 'Electronics': keeps 4 rows. - COUNT(*), SUM(stock): computed on those 4 rows only: 4 products, 277 units. - MIN(name): the alphabetically first name, 'Laptop Pro 14'. ### Common mistakes - Mixing an aggregate with a plain column, as in SELECT name, MAX(price) FROM products. The aggregate gives one row, so which name should appear? Some databases refuse; SQLite picks one for you, which is confusing. Keep plain columns out until you learn GROUP BY. - Expecting COUNT(column) to count NULLs. It skips them; use COUNT(*) to count rows. - Writing ROUND(AVG(price, 2)). The 2 belongs to ROUND: ROUND(AVG(price), 2). - Trying to filter on an aggregate in WHERE, such as WHERE COUNT(*) > 2. The next lesson shows the right tool, HAVING. ### Recap - Aggregate functions turn many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. - COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts different values. - ROUND(x, n) rounds to n decimals; functions can be nested. - WHERE filters rows first, then the aggregates summarise what is left.
sql-group: One total for the whole shop is a start, but the real question is usually "per something": orders per status, stock per category, customers per city. GROUP BY splits the rows into groups and runs the aggregate once per group. HAVING then lets you keep only some of the groups. ### GROUP BY: one result row per group ~~~sql SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY status; ~~~ - FROM orders: the 15 orders. - GROUP BY status: put orders with the same status into the same group. There are 4 statuses, so 4 groups. - SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n: for each group, show the status and count its rows. The result has 4 rows: cancelled 2, delivered 10, pending 1, shipped 2. The counts add up to 15, because every order belongs to exactly one group. ### The golden rule of GROUP BY Once you group, each result row stands for a whole group. So every column in SELECT must be either a column you grouped by (the same for the whole group) or an aggregate (one value summarising the group). ~~~sql SELECT category, SUM(stock) AS units, MAX(price) AS top_price FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY units DESC; ~~~ - GROUP BY category: 4 groups (Books, Electronics, Furniture, Grocery). - category: allowed, it is the grouping column. - SUM(stock), MAX(price): allowed, they are aggregates computed inside each group. - ORDER BY units DESC: sort the 4 result rows, largest stock first. ORDER BY can use the alias units. The result: Grocery 300 units (top price 18.9), Electronics 277 (1299), Books 95 (45), Furniture 83 (499). Adding name to SELECT would break the rule: a group of 4 products has 4 names, not one. ### Grouping by a column with NULL ~~~sql SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers FROM customers GROUP BY city; ~~~ - GROUP BY city: one group per city. All NULL cities form one group of their own. The result has 6 rows: an empty city with 1 customer (Farid Haddad), Bordeaux 1, Lyon 3, Marseille 1, Nantes 1, Paris 3. ### HAVING: filter the groups WHERE cannot test an aggregate, because WHERE runs before the groups exist. HAVING runs after grouping, so it can. ~~~sql SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers FROM customers GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2; ~~~ - GROUP BY city: the same 6 groups as before. - HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2: keep only the groups with at least 2 customers. The result has 2 rows: Lyon 3 and Paris 3. The other cities had a single customer and were dropped. ### WHERE and HAVING together Here is the full order in which the database works through a query: - FROM: read the table. - WHERE: keep only the matching rows. - GROUP BY: put the remaining rows into groups. - HAVING: keep only the matching groups. - SELECT: compute the columns, including aggregates and aliases. - ORDER BY: sort the result. - LIMIT: cut it. ~~~sql SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2; ~~~ - WHERE status <> 'cancelled': drop the 2 cancelled orders first, leaving 13. - GROUP BY customer_id: one group per customer who still has orders. - HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2: keep customers with at least 2 such orders. The result has 5 rows: customer 1 with 3 orders, and customers 2, 3, 7 and 8 with 2 each. Customer 5 placed 2 orders, but one was cancelled, so she falls out. ### Common mistakes - Putting a column in SELECT that is neither grouped nor aggregated. - Writing WHERE COUNT(*) > 2. Conditions on aggregates go in HAVING. - Writing HAVING before GROUP BY. The written order is SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT. - Using HAVING for plain row conditions. It works, but WHERE is clearer and filters earlier. ### Recap - GROUP BY column makes one result row per distinct value, and aggregates are computed per group. - In SELECT, use only grouped columns and aggregates. - WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. - Evaluation order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
sql-join: The orders table says order 4 belongs to customer 3, but who is customer 3? To answer "which customer placed each order?", you need data from two tables at once. A JOIN stitches rows of two tables together. ### Why data is split across tables Storing the customer's name and city on every order would repeat them again and again, and a change of address would mean editing many rows. Instead, each customer is stored once in customers, with a unique id. Each order only stores that number in its customer_id column. A column that points at the id of another table is called a foreign key. Joins follow these pointers. ### JOIN ... ON ~~~sql SELECT orders.id, orders.customer_id, customers.name FROM orders JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id; ~~~ - FROM orders: start with the 15 orders. - JOIN customers: bring in the customers table. - ON customers.id = orders.customer_id: the matching rule. An order row is glued to the customer row whose id equals the order's customer_id. - orders.id, customers.name: when two tables are involved, write table.column to say which table a column comes from. Both tables have an id and a name-like column, so this avoids confusion. The result has 15 rows: each order with its customer's name. Order 1 shows Alice Martin, order 4 shows Chloe Dubois. Alice appears 3 times because she placed 3 orders. ### Aliases for tables Typing full table names gets long. Give each table a short nickname, called an alias, right after its name. AS is optional here. ~~~sql SELECT o.id, c.name, o.status FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id; ~~~ - orders AS o: from now on, o means the orders table. - customers AS c: c means customers. Writing FROM orders o without AS works the same. - o.id, c.name, o.status: columns taken from each side. Same 15 rows as before, now with the status. Once you give a table an alias, use the alias everywhere in that query. ### Joining and filtering The joined rows behave like one wide table, so WHERE can test columns from either side. ~~~sql SELECT o.id, c.name, c.city FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.city = 'Paris'; ~~~ - JOIN ... ON: build the 15 joined rows. - WHERE c.city = 'Paris': keep orders whose customer lives in Paris. The result has 7 rows: orders 1, 3 and 12 from Alice Martin, 4 and 11 from Chloe Dubois, 10 and 15 from Hugo Bernard. ### Joining a link table order_items lists what is inside each order: one row per product in an order, with the quantity qty. Join it to products to see product names and prices. ~~~sql SELECT oi.order_id, p.name, oi.qty, p.price FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE oi.order_id = 8; ~~~ - FROM order_items oi: one row per line of an order. - JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id: attach each line's product. - WHERE oi.order_id = 8: look at order 8 only. The result has 2 rows: 4 Green Tea Box at 9.5 and 1 Coffee Beans 1kg at 18.9. ### What an inner join drops A plain JOIN is also called an inner join. It keeps only pairs that match. Ines Moreau and Jules Petit never ordered, so no order row points to them and they never appear in the results above. The next lesson shows how to keep them. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the ON clause, or comparing the wrong columns, such as c.id = o.id. Follow the foreign key: c.id = o.customer_id. - Writing id alone when both tables have an id. SQLite reports "ambiguous column name". - Using the full table name after giving it an alias. ### Recap - A foreign key column (like orders.customer_id) stores the id of a row in another table. - FROM a JOIN b ON b.id = a.b_id combines matching rows into one wider row. - Use table.column or alias.column to say where a column comes from. - An inner join keeps only rows that have a match on both sides.
sql-left: "Which customers have never ordered?" is a question about rows that have no match. An inner join cannot answer it, because it throws unmatched rows away. A LEFT JOIN keeps them. ### LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table The left table is the one written before the word JOIN (in FROM). The right table is the one after it. ~~~sql SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.status FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id; ~~~ - FROM customers c: the left table, 10 customers. - LEFT JOIN orders o: the right table. - ON o.customer_id = c.id: the same matching rule as an inner join. - Customers with one or more orders get one row per order, exactly like a normal join. - Customers with no order still get one row. The columns that would come from orders are filled with NULL. The result has 17 rows: the 15 orders with their customers, plus Ines Moreau and Jules Petit with an empty order_id and status. With a plain JOIN you would get only 15. ### Counting with a LEFT JOIN Because unmatched rows survive, you can count matches and get zero instead of losing the row. ~~~sql SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders_placed FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id; ~~~ - LEFT JOIN: the same 17 rows as above. - GROUP BY c.id: one group per customer. Grouping by the id is safer than by name, because two people can share a name. - COUNT(o.id): counts non-NULL order ids. For Ines and Jules the only value is NULL, so the count is 0. COUNT(*) would wrongly say 1, since it counts the row itself. The result has 10 rows: Alice Martin 3, David Kim 1, Ines Moreau 0, Jules Petit 0, and so on. ### Finding rows with no match After a LEFT JOIN, a row whose right side is NULL is a row that found no partner. Testing for that NULL in WHERE keeps exactly the unmatched rows. This pattern is often called an anti join. Here is a variation: which customers have never had an order delivered? ~~~sql SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'delivered' WHERE o.id IS NULL; ~~~ - LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'delivered': each customer is matched only with their delivered orders. The ON clause can hold several conditions. - WHERE o.id IS NULL: keep the customers for whom no delivered order was found. Every real order has an id, so a NULL id means "no match". - SELECT c.name: show who they are. The result has 3 rows: David Kim (his only order was cancelled), Ines Moreau and Jules Petit (no orders at all). ### ON versus WHERE The difference matters with LEFT JOIN. A condition in ON decides which right rows may match, and every left row is still kept. A condition on the right table in WHERE runs after the join and removes rows, including the NULL ones. ~~~sql SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'delivered'; ~~~ - WHERE o.status = 'delivered': rows where status is NULL fail this test, so the customers without orders vanish again. The result has 10 rows, the delivered orders only, and no row for Ines, Jules or David. The LEFT JOIN has quietly turned back into an inner join. Compare this with the previous example to see why the status test belonged in ON. ### Common mistakes - Swapping the tables. FROM orders LEFT JOIN customers keeps every order, not every customer. Put the table you want to keep in full on the left. - Testing = NULL instead of IS NULL. - Testing IS NULL on a column that can be NULL anyway (like a status). Test the right table's id, which is only NULL when there was no match. - Using COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN and getting 1 instead of 0. ### Recap - LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table; missing right side values become NULL. - LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL finds rows with no match. - Count matches with COUNT(right.column) to get 0 for unmatched rows. - Conditions on the right table belong in ON if you want to keep unmatched left rows.
sql-multi: "How much has each customer spent?" needs four tables: customers (the name), orders (who ordered and the status), order_items (what and how many) and products (the price). Joins can be chained, one after another, to walk from one table to the next. ### Following the path Each JOIN adds one table, linked to a table already in the query: - customers.id is stored in orders.customer_id - orders.id is stored in order_items.order_id - products.id is stored in order_items.product_id ~~~sql SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, p.name AS product, oi.qty FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE c.name = 'Alice Martin'; ~~~ - FROM customers c: start with customers. - JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id: attach each customer's orders. - JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id: attach the lines of each order. - JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id: attach the product of each line. - WHERE c.name = 'Alice Martin': look at one customer. - p.name AS product: two tables have a name column, so rename this one to avoid two columns called name. The result has 6 rows: one per product line in Alice's 3 orders (orders 1, 3 and 12). Each row is now one line item, the most detailed level, so customer and order information repeats. ### Line amounts: qty times price ~~~sql SELECT oi.order_id, p.name, oi.qty, p.price, oi.qty * p.price AS amount FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE oi.order_id IN (1, 8); ~~~ - oi.qty * p.price AS amount: for each line, quantity times unit price. - WHERE oi.order_id IN (1, 8): two orders only, to keep the result small. The result has 4 rows. Order 1: Laptop Pro 14, 1 x 1299 = 1299, and Wireless Mouse, 29.9. Order 8: Green Tea Box, 4 x 9.5 = 38, and Coffee Beans 1kg, 18.9. ### From line items to totals with GROUP BY Grouping on top of the joins turns line items into totals. Here: the value of each order. ~~~sql SELECT o.id, o.status, ROUND(SUM(oi.qty * p.price), 2) AS order_total FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY o.id ORDER BY order_total DESC LIMIT 5; ~~~ - The joins produce one row per line item (26 in the whole shop). - GROUP BY o.id: one group per order. - SUM(oi.qty * p.price): adds the line amounts of each order. ROUND(..., 2) keeps 2 decimals. - o.status: allowed in SELECT because it is the same for every row of one order, and SQLite accepts columns that depend on the grouped id. - ORDER BY order_total DESC LIMIT 5: the 5 biggest orders first. The result has 5 rows: order 9 (1548), order 1 (1328.9), order 4 (578.8), order 13 (499, cancelled) and order 7 (349). ### Filtering before grouping Cancelled orders should not count as sales. Filter them in WHERE, which runs before GROUP BY. Here: units sold per category. ~~~sql SELECT p.category, SUM(oi.qty) AS units_sold FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY p.category ORDER BY units_sold DESC; ~~~ - WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled': drop lines that belong to orders 5 and 13. - GROUP BY p.category: one row per category. - SUM(oi.qty): total units. The result has 4 rows: Grocery 12, Electronics 11, Books 7, Furniture 5. Without the WHERE, Electronics would show 12 and Furniture 6. ### Choosing what to group by Group by the thing each result row should represent: GROUP BY o.id for one row per order, GROUP BY c.id for one row per customer. Grouping by an id is safer than grouping by a name. With GROUP BY c.id you can still show c.name, because each id has exactly one name. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting a link in the chain, for example joining products straight to orders. There is no product column in orders; you must go through order_items. - Joining on the wrong column, such as oi.order_id = c.id. Each ON should follow one foreign key. - Summing p.price alone and forgetting the quantity. - Filtering cancelled orders in HAVING instead of WHERE. The status belongs to rows, so test it in WHERE. ### Recap - Chain joins to walk across tables: each JOIN ... ON follows one foreign key. - After the joins, each row is one line item; qty * price is its amount. - GROUP BY on top turns line items into totals per order, per customer or per category. - Filter rows with WHERE before grouping; sort totals with ORDER BY alias DESC.
sql-self: In the employees table, each person has a manager_id that holds the id of another employee. To answer "who is each person's manager?", the table has to be joined to itself. That is called a self join. ### Two aliases, one table A self join uses the same table twice, under two different aliases. Think of them as two copies: one plays the role of the employee, the other the role of the manager. ~~~sql SELECT e.name, e.title, m.name AS manager_name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id; ~~~ - FROM employees e: the first copy, e for employee. - JOIN employees m: the second copy, m for manager. - ON m.id = e.manager_id: pair each employee with the row whose id equals their manager_id. - m.name AS manager_name: without a new name, two result columns would both be called name. The result has 7 rows, for example Tom Girard with manager Marc Durand, and Paul Lambert with Tom Girard. Sofia Laurent, the CEO, is missing: her manager_id is NULL, so the inner join finds no partner for her. Aliases are mandatory here; employees.name would not say which copy you mean. ### Comparing a row with its manager Once each employee sits next to their manager, you can compare their values. ~~~sql SELECT e.name, e.salary, m.name AS manager_name, m.salary AS manager_salary, m.salary - e.salary AS gap FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id ORDER BY gap DESC; ~~~ - m.salary - e.salary AS gap: how much more the manager earns. - ORDER BY gap DESC: biggest gap first. The result has 7 rows. Lea Fontaine earns 85000 more than Yann Bonnet, her accountant, which is the biggest gap. Tom Girard earns 23000 more than Paul Lambert, the smallest. ### Counting direct reports ~~~sql SELECT m.name AS manager_name, COUNT(*) AS direct_reports FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id GROUP BY m.id; ~~~ - The join gives one row per employee who has a manager. - GROUP BY m.id: one group per manager. - COUNT(*): how many employees point to that manager. The result has 4 rows: Sofia Laurent 2, Marc Durand 1, Lea Fontaine 2, Tom Girard 2. ### LEFT self join: keep everyone A LEFT JOIN works on a self join exactly as on two different tables: every row of the left copy is kept, and NULL fills the right side when there is no match. Here the question is turned around: for each person, list who reports to them, including people with nobody under them. ~~~sql SELECT m.name AS person, r.name AS reports_to_them FROM employees m LEFT JOIN employees r ON r.manager_id = m.id ORDER BY m.id; ~~~ - FROM employees m: the left copy, every person (8 rows). - LEFT JOIN employees r ON r.manager_id = m.id: attach each person's direct reports, if any. - ORDER BY m.id: list people in id order. The result has 11 rows. Sofia Laurent, Lea Fontaine and Tom Girard appear twice (2 reports each), Marc Durand once. Nina Roux, Paul Lambert, Zoe Mercier and Yann Bonnet appear once each with an empty second column: nobody reports to them. The side of the table you want to keep in full goes on the left. ### Pairs from the same table A self join can also pair rows that share something, such as colleagues with the same manager. ~~~sql SELECT a.name, b.name AS colleague FROM employees a JOIN employees b ON a.manager_id = b.manager_id AND a.id < b.id; ~~~ - ON a.manager_id = b.manager_id: same manager. - AND a.id < b.id: avoid pairing someone with themselves, and avoid listing each pair twice. The result has 3 pairs: Marc Durand and Lea Fontaine, Nina Roux and Yann Bonnet, Paul Lambert and Zoe Mercier. ### Common mistakes - Using only one alias, or none. Each copy needs its own alias. - Reversing the ON condition (e.id = m.manager_id), which swaps the roles: you get reports instead of managers. - Forgetting to rename columns, ending up with two columns called name. - Expecting the top of the hierarchy to appear with an inner join. ### Recap - A self join joins a table to itself, using two aliases for two roles. - JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id places each employee next to their manager. - An inner self join drops rows with a NULL link; a LEFT self join keeps them with NULL on the right. - Rename columns with AS so the result stays readable.
sql-sub: "Who earns more than the average?" needs two steps: first compute the average, then compare each salary with it. A subquery lets you do both in one statement: it is a complete query written inside another one, between parentheses. The inner query runs to produce a value or a list, and the outer query uses it. ### A subquery that returns one value ~~~sql SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees); ~~~ - (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees): the inner query. It returns a single value, the average salary: 103000. - WHERE salary > (...): the outer query compares each employee's salary with that value, as if you had typed 103000 yourself. - SELECT name, salary: show who passed the test. The result has 3 rows: Sofia Laurent (180000), Marc Durand (150000) and Lea Fontaine (140000). A subquery that returns exactly one value (one row, one column) is called a scalar subquery. You can use it anywhere a single number would fit. You could not write WHERE salary > AVG(salary), because aggregates are not allowed in WHERE: the subquery is the way around that. ### A scalar subquery in SELECT ~~~sql SELECT name, salary, salary - (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) AS vs_average FROM employees; ~~~ - salary - (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees): for each row, subtract the average from the salary. - AS vs_average: name the result. The result has 8 rows. Sofia Laurent is 77000 above the average; Yann Bonnet is 48000 below it, shown as -48000. ### IN with a subquery: membership in a list When the inner query returns one column with several rows, it acts as a list, and you can use it with IN. ~~~sql SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped'); ~~~ - (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped'): returns the customer ids of shipped orders: 2 and 1. - WHERE id IN (...): keep customers whose id is in that list. The result has 2 rows: Alice Martin and Bruno Silva. NOT IN (...) does the opposite. Be careful: if the inner list contains a NULL, NOT IN returns no rows at all, because nothing can be proved different from an unknown value. ### EXISTS: is there at least one matching row? EXISTS (subquery) is true when the inner query returns at least one row, and false when it returns none. NOT EXISTS is the reverse. The inner query can refer to the current row of the outer query; this is called a correlated subquery, because it is re-run for each outer row. ~~~sql SELECT name, city FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status <> 'cancelled' ); ~~~ - FROM customers c: the outer query, one customer at a time. - SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ...: look for a non-cancelled order of this customer. c.id comes from the outer query. SELECT 1 is a convention: EXISTS only cares whether a row exists, not what it contains. - WHERE NOT EXISTS (...): keep the customer when no such order was found. The result has 3 rows: David Kim, Ines Moreau and Jules Petit. ### Correlated comparison: above the average of its own group ~~~sql SELECT name, category, price FROM products p WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category); ~~~ - products p and products p2: the same table twice, with different aliases, so the inner query can refer to the outer row. - WHERE p2.category = p.category: the average is computed only over the current product's category. The result has 5 rows: the products priced above their own category's average, such as Laptop Pro 14 in Electronics and SQL Cookbook in Books. ### A subquery in FROM A subquery can also stand in for a table. It must have parentheses and is often given an alias. ~~~sql SELECT dept, avg_salary FROM (SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY dept) AS d WHERE avg_salary > 90000; ~~~ - (SELECT dept, AVG(salary) ... GROUP BY dept) AS d: a temporary table with one row per department. - WHERE avg_salary > 90000: filter those rows like any table. The result has 2 rows: Exec (180000) and Tech (96750). ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the parentheses around the subquery. - Using = with a subquery that returns several rows. Use IN for lists. - Using a scalar subquery that returns several values. It must return exactly one. - Using NOT IN on a list that may contain NULL. NOT EXISTS is safer. ### Recap - A subquery is a query in parentheses inside another query. - A scalar subquery returns one value and can be compared with >, = and so on. - IN (subquery) tests membership in a list; EXISTS tests whether any row matches. - A correlated subquery refers to the outer row and is evaluated once per row.
sql-cte: As questions grow, subqueries inside subqueries become hard to read. A common table expression, or CTE, solves this: you name an intermediate result with WITH, then use it by name in the main query, as if it were a table. You build the answer in readable steps, like a recipe. ### WITH: name a step ~~~sql WITH order_sizes AS ( SELECT order_id, SUM(qty) AS items FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id ) SELECT order_id, items FROM order_sizes WHERE items >= 3; ~~~ - WITH order_sizes AS ( ... ): define a temporary result called order_sizes. Inside the parentheses is an ordinary query. - SELECT order_id, SUM(qty) AS items ... GROUP BY order_id: one row per order with its number of items (15 rows). - SELECT ... FROM order_sizes: the main query reads the CTE like a table. - WHERE items >= 3: keep orders with 3 items or more. The result has 8 rows: orders 3, 4, 6, 8 (5 items), 11, 12, 14 and 15. A CTE only exists while this one statement runs; nothing is saved in the database. The main query comes right after the closing parenthesis, with no semicolon in between. ### Dates with strftime In this database, dates are text such as '2025-03-15'. SQLite's strftime(format, date) function extracts or reformats parts of a date. In the format, %Y is the 4 digit year, %m the 2 digit month and %d the day. Any other characters, like the dash, are copied as they are. ~~~sql SELECT order_date, strftime('%Y', order_date) AS year, strftime('%m', order_date) AS month_number, strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS year_month FROM orders LIMIT 3; ~~~ - strftime('%Y', order_date): '2025'. - strftime('%m', order_date): '01' for January. - strftime('%Y-%m', order_date): '2025-01', the year and month together. This is the handy one for monthly reports, because it sorts correctly as text. The result has 3 rows, orders from January 2025. Other helpers: date('now') gives today's date, and julianday(a) - julianday(b) gives the number of days between two dates. ### A CTE with a monthly grouping Calculated columns can be named inside the CTE, then grouped in the main query. ~~~sql WITH dated AS ( SELECT id, strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month FROM orders ) SELECT month, COUNT(*) AS orders_placed FROM dated GROUP BY month ORDER BY month; ~~~ - The CTE dated: one row per order with its month label. Naming the expression month here keeps the main query short. - GROUP BY month: one group per month. - ORDER BY month: '2025-01' before '2025-02', and so on. The result has 5 rows: January 3, February 3, March 4, April 4, May 1. Together that makes the 15 orders. ### Joins inside a CTE A CTE can contain anything a query can: joins, WHERE, GROUP BY. Here the first step computes the value of every non-cancelled order. ~~~sql WITH order_totals AS ( SELECT o.id, ROUND(SUM(oi.qty * p.price), 2) AS total FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY o.id ) SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS avg_order, MAX(total) AS biggest FROM order_totals; ~~~ - The CTE: one row per non-cancelled order, with its total (13 rows). - The main query: aggregates over those 13 totals. The result has 1 row: 13 orders, an average order of 367.4, and a biggest order of 1548. Computing "the average of the totals" in a single query without a step would be awkward; with a CTE, it reads naturally. ### Several CTEs, and reusing one Separate several CTEs with commas, after a single WITH. A later step can read an earlier one, and a CTE can be read more than once. ~~~sql WITH order_totals AS ( SELECT o.id, SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS total FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY o.id ), average AS ( SELECT AVG(total) AS avg_total FROM order_totals ) SELECT o.id, ROUND(o.total, 2) AS total FROM order_totals o, average a WHERE o.total > a.avg_total; ~~~ - order_totals: the same first step. - average AS (...): a second step that reads the first and returns one row. - FROM order_totals o, average a: a comma between two tables pairs every row of one with every row of the other. Since average has a single row, this simply attaches it to each order. - WHERE o.total > a.avg_total: keep orders above the average. The result has 3 rows: orders 1, 4 and 9. ### Common mistakes - Putting a semicolon between the CTE and the main query. The whole thing is one statement. - Writing WITH twice. Use one WITH and separate CTEs with commas. - Forgetting to name a calculated column inside the CTE, then having no clean name to use outside it. - Writing strftime('%Y-%M', ...). Capital %M means minutes; the month is lower case %m. ### Recap - WITH name AS (query) names an intermediate result; the main query reads it like a table. - Several CTEs: WITH a AS (...), b AS (...) SELECT ...; later ones can use earlier ones. - strftime('%Y-%m', date) turns a date into a year-month label for monthly reports. - A CTE can hold joins, filters and grouping, then be aggregated again outside.
sql-window: "Rank each employee within their department" or "show each salary next to its department average" are hard with GROUP BY, because grouping collapses the rows: you lose the individual employees. Window functions compute over a set of related rows but keep every row in the result. ### OVER: an aggregate that keeps the rows Add OVER (...) after a function to turn it into a window function. The parentheses describe the window: which rows the function looks at for the current row. ~~~sql SELECT name, dept, salary, AVG(salary) OVER () AS company_avg FROM employees; ~~~ - AVG(salary) OVER (): empty parentheses mean the window is the whole result. Every row gets the average of all salaries. - No GROUP BY: all 8 employees stay in the result. The result has 8 rows, each showing 103000 as company_avg. A plain AVG(salary) would have returned a single row instead. ### PARTITION BY: one window per group PARTITION BY column splits the rows into groups, like GROUP BY, but without collapsing them. The function is computed inside each group. ~~~sql SELECT name, dept, salary, ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept)) AS dept_avg, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_size FROM employees; ~~~ - PARTITION BY dept: three windows: Exec (1 person), Finance (3) and Tech (4). - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept): each row gets its own department's average. ROUND tidies it. - COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY dept): each row gets its department's head count. The result has 8 rows. The Finance employees show 85667.0 and 3, the Tech employees 96750.0 and 4. ### RANK with ORDER BY inside the window Ranking functions number rows in an order. The order goes inside OVER. ~~~sql SELECT name, dept, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank_in_dept FROM employees; ~~~ - RANK(): gives 1 to the first row of each window, 2 to the next, and so on. It takes no argument; the order comes from OVER. - PARTITION BY dept: restart the numbering in each department. - ORDER BY salary DESC: highest salary first, so the best paid person in each department gets 1. The result has 8 rows. In Tech: Marc Durand 1, Tom Girard 2, Paul Lambert 3, Zoe Mercier 4. In Finance: Lea Fontaine 1, Nina Roux 2, Yann Bonnet 3. Sofia Laurent is 1 in Exec. Without PARTITION BY, the ranking would run across the whole company. ### Ties: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK The three ranking functions differ only when two rows tie. ~~~sql WITH counts AS ( SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ) SELECT customer_id, n, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY n DESC) AS row_num, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY n DESC) AS rnk, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY n DESC) AS dense FROM counts; ~~~ - The CTE counts orders per customer: customer 1 has 3, five customers have 2, two have 1. - ROW_NUMBER(): 1, 2, 3, ... with no repeats, even for ties. Who gets which number among tied rows is not guaranteed. - RANK(): tied rows share a rank, then the next rank skips: 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 7, 7. - DENSE_RANK(): tied rows share a rank, with no gap: 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3. The result has 8 rows, one per customer who ordered. ### Running totals When the window has an ORDER BY, aggregate functions become cumulative: each row sees the rows from the start up to itself. ~~~sql SELECT id, order_date, COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS orders_so_far FROM orders LIMIT 6; ~~~ - COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY order_date): for each order, count the orders on or before its date. The first 6 rows show orders_so_far going 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The same idea with SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date) gives a running revenue total. ### When window functions run Window functions are computed in the SELECT step, after FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING. So WHERE cannot filter on them: WHERE rank_in_dept = 1 fails, because the rank does not exist yet when WHERE runs. To filter on a rank, compute it in a CTE first, then filter in the main query. The boss lesson uses exactly that. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting OVER after RANK(), ROW_NUMBER() or DENSE_RANK(). They only exist as window functions. - Putting the ORDER BY of the ranking at the end of the query instead of inside OVER. The final ORDER BY only sorts the display. - Forgetting PARTITION BY and ranking across the whole table. - Ordering ascending when "1 = biggest" is wanted. Use DESC. ### Recap - function() OVER (...) computes across related rows but keeps every row. - PARTITION BY sets the groups; ORDER BY inside OVER sets the order within each group. - ROW_NUMBER never ties, RANK ties and skips, DENSE_RANK ties without gaps. - Window functions run in SELECT, so filter on them in an outer query or a CTE.
sql-rec: "Who is in Tom Girard's chain of command, all the way up to the CEO?" is a question of unknown depth: a self join climbs one level, two self joins climb two levels, but how many do you need? A recursive CTE repeats a step until there is nothing left to find. It is the standard tool for trees and hierarchies: org charts, category trees, parts made of parts. ### UNION ALL: stacking results Recursive CTEs rely on UNION ALL, which stacks the rows of two queries on top of each other. Both queries must return the same number of columns, in the same order. ~~~sql SELECT name, 'customer' AS kind FROM customers WHERE city = 'Nantes' UNION ALL SELECT name, 'employee' AS kind FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Exec'; ~~~ - The first query: 1 row, Jules Petit. - UNION ALL: append the next query's rows below. - The second query: 1 row, Sofia Laurent. The result has 2 rows. The column names come from the first query. UNION without ALL does the same but removes duplicate rows. ### WITH RECURSIVE: counting from 1 to 5 ~~~sql WITH RECURSIVE n(x) AS ( SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 5 ) SELECT x FROM n; ~~~ - WITH RECURSIVE n(x): a CTE named n with one column named x. The column list in parentheses after the name sets the column names. - SELECT 1: the anchor. It runs once and gives the starting rows: here a single row, x = 1. - UNION ALL: stack the anchor and every later round together. - SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 5: the recursive step. It reads the rows produced by the previous round (from n, the CTE itself) and makes new ones. From 1 it makes 2, from 2 it makes 3, and so on. - WHERE x < 5: the stop condition. When x reaches 5, the step produces no row and the recursion ends. The result has 5 rows: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Without the stop condition, the query would never end. ### Walking a hierarchy upwards Each round can join the table to the rows found in the previous round. Here we start at one employee and climb from manager to manager. ~~~sql WITH RECURSIVE bosses(id, name, manager_id, step) AS ( SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 FROM employees WHERE name = 'Paul Lambert' UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, b.step + 1 FROM employees e JOIN bosses b ON e.id = b.manager_id ) SELECT name, step FROM bosses; ~~~ - Anchor: Paul Lambert, with step 0. - Recursive step: find the employee whose id equals the manager_id of the row found last time. That is Paul's manager, then that person's manager, and so on. - b.step + 1: each round adds one to the step counter, so you can see how far up each row is. - The recursion stops by itself at Sofia Laurent: her manager_id is NULL, so the join finds nobody. The result has 4 rows: Paul Lambert 0, Tom Girard 1, Marc Durand 2, Sofia Laurent 3. ### Walking downwards To go the other way, from the top down, start the anchor at the top row and swap the join condition: find employees whose manager_id equals the id of a row found in the previous round. Each round then reaches one level deeper. The anchor can also select several rows, for example everyone whose manager_id IS NULL. ### Generating a series of dates Recursion is also handy to produce rows that are not in any table, like every month of a year. ~~~sql WITH RECURSIVE months(m) AS ( SELECT '2025-01-01' UNION ALL SELECT date(m, '+1 month') FROM months WHERE m < '2025-05-01' ) SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', m) AS month FROM months; ~~~ - Anchor: the first of January 2025. - date(m, '+1 month'): SQLite's date function adds one month to a date. - WHERE m < '2025-05-01': stop after May. The result has 5 rows, '2025-01' to '2025-05'. Such a list can be LEFT JOINed to real data to show months with zero sales. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting RECURSIVE after WITH. SQLite then complains that the CTE does not exist yet. - No stop condition, so the query runs forever. Make sure each round eventually finds nothing. - Different column counts in the anchor and the recursive step. - Reversing the join direction, so you walk up instead of down. ### Recap - UNION ALL stacks rows from queries with the same columns. - WITH RECURSIVE name(columns) AS (anchor UNION ALL step): the anchor runs once, then the step repeats on the previous round's rows until it returns nothing. - Joining the table to the CTE walks a hierarchy one level per round; a counter column like step + 1 tracks the depth.
sql-dml: So far, every query only read data. Running a shop also means changing it: a new customer signs up, prices change, a mistaken order must go. Three statements do this: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes rows and DELETE removes rows. Each example below ends with a SELECT so you can see the effect. The page runs them on a fresh copy, so nothing is broken for the next example. ### INSERT: add a row ~~~sql INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, joined) VALUES ('Lou Garnier', 'lou@mail.com', 'Lille', '2025-02-01'); SELECT * FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lille'; ~~~ - INSERT INTO customers: add a row to the customers table. - (name, email, city, joined): the columns you are about to fill, in this order. - VALUES ('Lou Garnier', ...): the values, in the same order as the column list. Text and dates in quotes. - The id column is not listed. Because it is the table's INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, SQLite fills it automatically with the next number. The SELECT shows 1 row: Lou Garnier with id 11, since the table already had ids 1 to 10. Each statement ends with a semicolon, so several can follow each other. ### INSERT several rows at once ~~~sql INSERT INTO products (name, category, price, stock) VALUES ('Notebook A5', 'Books', 6.5, 300), ('Pen Set', 'Books', 12.0, 120); SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE id > 10; ~~~ - VALUES (...), (...): one pair of parentheses per row, separated by commas. The SELECT shows 4 rows: the existing products 11 and 12, then the new Notebook A5 (id 13) and Pen Set (id 14). ### UPDATE: change existing rows ~~~sql UPDATE products SET price = ROUND(price * 0.9, 2) WHERE category = 'Grocery'; SELECT name, category, price FROM products WHERE category = 'Grocery'; ~~~ - UPDATE products: the table to change. - SET price = ROUND(price * 0.9, 2): the new value. On the right, price means the current value of that row, so this is a 10% discount, rounded to 2 decimals. You can set several columns: SET price = 10, stock = 5. - WHERE category = 'Grocery': which rows to change. Only these 2 rows are touched. The SELECT shows Coffee Beans 1kg going from 18.9 to 17.01, and Green Tea Box from 9.5 to 8.55. A price increase works the same way, with a factor above 1: price * 1.05 is a 5% rise. ### DELETE: remove rows ~~~sql DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending'; SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY status; ~~~ - DELETE FROM orders: remove rows from orders. No column list: DELETE always removes whole rows. - WHERE status = 'pending': only the rows matching this condition. The SELECT shows 14 orders left: cancelled 2, delivered 10, shipped 2. The pending order 10 is gone. Its lines in order_items are still there, because SQLite does not remove related rows unless the tables were set up to do so. ### Always look before you change An UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE changes every row in the table, and there is no undo button. A safe habit: write the SELECT with the same WHERE first, check the rows it returns, then turn it into the UPDATE or DELETE. ~~~sql SELECT id, customer_id, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped'; ~~~ - This shows exactly which rows a DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped' would remove: 2 rows, orders 7 and 12. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting WHERE in UPDATE or DELETE, and changing the whole table. - Listing a different number of columns and values in INSERT. - Writing SET price * 0.9. SET always needs column = new value. - Writing DELETE * FROM .... DELETE takes no column list. ### Recap - INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values), (values); adds rows; an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY id fills itself. - UPDATE table SET column = expression WHERE condition; changes matching rows; the expression can use the current value. - DELETE FROM table WHERE condition; removes matching rows. - Run the matching SELECT first: without WHERE, every row is affected.
sql-create: The shop wants to track suppliers, so it needs a new table. CREATE TABLE defines one: its name, its columns, the type of data each column holds, and the rules, called constraints, that every row must follow. The database then refuses any write that breaks a rule, whichever app or person tries it. ### CREATE TABLE: columns and types ~~~sql CREATE TABLE suppliers ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, country TEXT DEFAULT 'FR', rating INTEGER CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5), lead_days INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (lead_days > 0), product_id INTEGER REFERENCES products(id) ); INSERT INTO suppliers (name, rating, lead_days, product_id) VALUES ('TechSource', 4, 7, 1); INSERT INTO suppliers (name, country, lead_days) VALUES ('Paper House', 'BE', 3); SELECT * FROM suppliers; ~~~ - CREATE TABLE suppliers ( ... ): the new table's name, then one line per column inside parentheses, separated by commas. No comma after the last column. - Each column line is: name, then type, then any constraints. The common SQLite types are INTEGER (whole numbers), REAL (decimal numbers) and TEXT. - id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY: the primary key identifies each row uniquely. In SQLite, an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is filled automatically when you leave it out. - name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE: NOT NULL makes the value required; UNIQUE forbids two rows with the same value. A column can carry several constraints, one after another. - country TEXT DEFAULT 'FR': DEFAULT gives the value used when an INSERT does not mention the column. - rating INTEGER CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5): CHECK (condition) rejects any row where the condition is false. - lead_days INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (lead_days > 0): required, and must be positive. - product_id INTEGER REFERENCES products(id): a foreign key, declaring that the value should be the id of a row in products. The SELECT shows 2 rows. TechSource got id 1 and country 'FR' from the DEFAULT. Paper House got id 2, country 'BE', and NULL for rating and product_id, which is allowed because those columns are not NOT NULL. A CHECK lets NULL through; add NOT NULL as well if the value is required. ### Checking the structure SQLite can describe a table's columns. pragma_table_info('table') can be read like a table, with one row per column. ~~~sql CREATE TABLE suppliers ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, lead_days INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (lead_days > 0), note TEXT ); SELECT name, type, "notnull", pk FROM pragma_table_info('suppliers'); ~~~ - name, type: each column's name and declared type. - "notnull": 1 when the column is NOT NULL. The double quotes are needed because notnull is also an SQL keyword; double quotes mark a name, single quotes mark text. - pk: 1 for the primary key column. The result has 4 rows: id (pk 1), name (notnull 1), lead_days (notnull 1) and note (both 0). This is a quick way to check that a table was created exactly as intended. ### What a constraint violation looks like A write that breaks a rule stops with an error and changes nothing. These statements would each fail on the first example's table: ~~~text INSERT INTO suppliers (name, lead_days) VALUES ('TechSource', 5); -- UNIQUE constraint failed: suppliers.name INSERT INTO suppliers (rating, lead_days) VALUES (3, 5); -- NOT NULL constraint failed: suppliers.name INSERT INTO suppliers (name, rating, lead_days) VALUES ('Acme', 9, 5); -- CHECK constraint failed: rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5 ~~~ ### Seeing constraints at work without an error INSERT OR IGNORE skips any row that breaks a constraint instead of stopping with an error. It is a handy way to watch the rules filter data. ~~~sql CREATE TABLE suppliers ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, rating INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5) ); INSERT OR IGNORE INTO suppliers (name, rating) VALUES ('Good Co', 5), ('Good Co', 4), (NULL, 3), ('Bad Rating Ltd', 7), ('Fine Inc', 1); SELECT * FROM suppliers; ~~~ - ('Good Co', 4): rejected by UNIQUE, the name already exists. - (NULL, 3): rejected by NOT NULL on name. - ('Bad Rating Ltd', 7): rejected by the CHECK. The SELECT shows only 2 rows: Good Co (5) and Fine Inc (1). ### About foreign keys in SQLite REFERENCES products(id) documents the link and lets tools understand it. SQLite only enforces it, refusing a product_id that does not exist, after the command PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; has been run on the connection. Most other databases enforce it always. Constraints and REFERENCES can be combined on one column, for example INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id). ### Common mistakes - A comma after the last column, or a missing comma between two columns. - Putting constraints before the type. The order is name, type, constraints. - Forgetting the parentheses around a CHECK condition. - Using double quotes for text values. Double quotes are for names, single quotes for text. ### Recap - CREATE TABLE name (column TYPE constraints, ...); defines a table. - PRIMARY KEY identifies rows; NOT NULL requires a value; UNIQUE forbids duplicates; DEFAULT fills missing values; CHECK (condition) enforces a rule. - REFERENCES table(id) declares a foreign key. - pragma_table_info('table') shows the structure you created.
sql-view: Some queries get run again and again: "our Paris customers", "the value of each order". A view saves a query under a name so anyone can reuse it like a table. An index is a different tool: it makes searches on a column faster. ### CREATE VIEW: save a query ~~~sql CREATE VIEW paris_customers AS SELECT id, name, email FROM customers WHERE city = 'Paris'; SELECT * FROM paris_customers; ~~~ - CREATE VIEW paris_customers AS: the name of the view, then AS. - SELECT id, name, email FROM customers WHERE city = 'Paris': the query the view stands for. Its columns become the view's columns. - SELECT * FROM paris_customers: you read a view exactly like a table. The result has 3 rows: Alice Martin, Chloe Dubois and Hugo Bernard. A view stores no data. It stores only the query, which runs again each time you read the view. ### A view over joins and grouping Views shine when they hide a long query. Here, the value of every order with its customer's name. ~~~sql CREATE VIEW order_values AS SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, o.status, ROUND(SUM(oi.qty * p.price), 2) AS total FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY o.id; SELECT customer, order_id, total FROM order_values WHERE status = 'delivered' AND total > 500 ORDER BY total DESC; ~~~ - CREATE VIEW order_values AS ...: the four table join and GROUP BY from earlier lessons, saved once. Every column gets a clear name with AS, because those names are what users of the view will type. - FROM order_values WHERE ... ORDER BY ...: the reader of the view only needs a simple query. WHERE, ORDER BY, joins and GROUP BY all work on a view. The result has 3 rows: Grace Lee's order 9 (1548), Alice Martin's order 1 (1328.9) and Chloe Dubois's order 4 (578.8). ### A view is always up to date ~~~sql CREATE VIEW paris_customers AS SELECT id, name, email FROM customers WHERE city = 'Paris'; UPDATE customers SET city = 'Paris' WHERE name = 'Grace Lee'; SELECT * FROM paris_customers; ~~~ - The view is created first. - The UPDATE moves Grace Lee to Paris, in the customers table. - Reading the view runs its query again, so it sees the change. The result now has 4 rows, Grace Lee included. You never need to refresh a view. In SQLite, views are read only: you change the data in the underlying tables. DROP VIEW name; deletes a view, without touching the tables. ### CREATE INDEX: faster lookups Without an index, finding the rows WHERE category = 'Books' means reading every row of the table. An index is a sorted list of a column's values with pointers to their rows, like the index at the back of a book. With it, the database jumps straight to the matching rows. On 12 rows you will not notice, but on millions of rows it is the difference between milliseconds and minutes. ~~~sql CREATE INDEX idx_products_category ON products(category); SELECT name, tbl_name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index'; ~~~ - CREATE INDEX idx_products_category: the index name. A common convention is idx_table_column. - ON products(category): the table, then the column or columns in parentheses. - sqlite_master: a built-in table where SQLite lists every table, view, index and trigger in the database, with its type, name and tbl_name (the table it belongs to). The result has 2 rows: sqlite_autoindex_customers_1, which SQLite created by itself for the UNIQUE email column, and the new idx_products_category on products. Queries do not mention the index: the database decides to use it on its own. ### When to add an index Index columns you often filter on (WHERE), join on (ON) or sort by, especially foreign keys like orders.customer_id or order_items.order_id. Do not index everything: each index takes space and slows down INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE a little, because it must be kept up to date. DROP INDEX name; removes one. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting AS after the view name. - Leaving calculated columns unnamed in a view, which makes them awkward to use. - Expecting a view to store a snapshot of the data. It always re-runs its query. - Writing CREATE INDEX ON products(category) without a name. SQLite requires one. ### Recap - CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...; saves a query; read it with SELECT ... FROM name. - A view stores no data and is always current. - CREATE INDEX name ON table(column); speeds up searches, joins and sorts on that column. - sqlite_master lists the objects in the database.
sql-trigger: Some things must happen every time data changes, whoever changes it: lower the stock when an item is sold, keep a log when something is deleted, record each status change. A trigger is SQL that the database runs automatically when a given change happens on a table. No application code has to remember to do it. ### An AFTER INSERT trigger with NEW ~~~sql CREATE TRIGGER reduce_stock AFTER INSERT ON order_items BEGIN UPDATE products SET stock = stock - NEW.qty WHERE id = NEW.product_id; END; INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES (15, 2, 3); SELECT id, name, stock FROM products WHERE id = 2; ~~~ - CREATE TRIGGER reduce_stock: the trigger's name. - AFTER INSERT ON order_items: when it fires. The event can be INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, and the timing BEFORE or AFTER the change. - BEGIN ... END: the body, one or more SQL statements, each ending with a semicolon. END also gets its own semicolon. - NEW.qty, NEW.product_id: inside the trigger, NEW is the row being inserted, so NEW.column reads its values. - The trigger runs once for each row inserted. The SELECT shows the Wireless Mouse with stock 147: it had 150, and the trigger subtracted the 3 just sold. Nobody wrote that UPDATE by hand. ### OLD: the row before the change OLD is the row as it was before the change. It exists in UPDATE and DELETE triggers. NEW exists in INSERT and UPDATE triggers. An UPDATE trigger has both, so it can compare before and after. ~~~sql CREATE TABLE deleted_customers (id INTEGER, name TEXT, email TEXT); CREATE TRIGGER keep_deleted AFTER DELETE ON customers BEGIN INSERT INTO deleted_customers (id, name, email) VALUES (OLD.id, OLD.name, OLD.email); END; DELETE FROM customers WHERE city = 'Nantes'; SELECT * FROM deleted_customers; ~~~ - CREATE TABLE deleted_customers: a log table to hold copies. - AFTER DELETE ON customers: fire after each deleted customer row. - VALUES (OLD.id, OLD.name, OLD.email): copy the values of the row that was just removed. The SELECT shows 1 row: Jules Petit, id 10, the only customer in Nantes. The row is gone from customers but kept in the log. ### UPDATE OF a column, and WHEN Two options narrow down when an update trigger fires: - AFTER UPDATE OF status ON orders: fire only when an UPDATE statement sets the status column. Updates of other columns are ignored. - WHEN condition, written before BEGIN: fire only if the condition is true for that row. It can use OLD and NEW. ~~~sql CREATE TABLE status_log ( order_id INTEGER, old_status TEXT, new_status TEXT, changed_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ); CREATE TRIGGER log_status AFTER UPDATE OF status ON orders WHEN OLD.status <> NEW.status BEGIN INSERT INTO status_log (order_id, old_status, new_status) VALUES (NEW.id, OLD.status, NEW.status); END; UPDATE orders SET status = 'delivered' WHERE status = 'shipped'; UPDATE orders SET status = status WHERE id = 1; SELECT * FROM status_log; ~~~ - changed_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP: CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is the current date and time. As a DEFAULT, it stamps each log row automatically, since the INSERT does not mention that column. - AFTER UPDATE OF status ON orders: only updates that set status. - WHEN OLD.status <> NEW.status: only when the value really changed. - The first UPDATE changes orders 7 and 12 from shipped to delivered: 2 log rows. - The second UPDATE sets order 1's status to the value it already had. The trigger is considered, but WHEN is false, so nothing is logged. The SELECT shows 2 rows, for orders 7 and 12, each with 'shipped', 'delivered' and the current time in UTC. ### Listing and removing triggers ~~~sql CREATE TRIGGER reduce_stock AFTER INSERT ON order_items BEGIN UPDATE products SET stock = stock - NEW.qty WHERE id = NEW.product_id; END; SELECT type, name, tbl_name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'trigger'; ~~~ - sqlite_master lists triggers too, with the table each one watches. The result has 1 row: reduce_stock on order_items. DROP TRIGGER name; removes a trigger. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the semicolons inside BEGIN ... END, or the final END;. - Using NEW in a DELETE trigger or OLD in an INSERT trigger. Those rows do not exist there. - Putting WHEN after BEGIN.
