It goes between the event line and BEGIN. - Comparing with = when you want "changed": use OLD.col <> NEW.col. ### Recap - CREATE TRIGGER name AFTER|BEFORE INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE ON table BEGIN ...; END; runs SQL automatically on each changed row. - NEW is the row after the change, OLD the row before it. - UPDATE OF column limits the trigger to one column; WHEN condition adds a test. - DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP stamps log rows with the time.
sql-boss: Real reporting questions combine everything you have learned. "Who is the top earner in each department?" or "what is the most expensive product in each category?" need a ranking inside groups, then a filter that keeps only the winners. The recipe is: gather and aggregate the data in a CTE, rank it with a window function in a second step, then keep rank 1. ### Why you need a CTE to filter on a rank Window functions are computed in the SELECT step, after WHERE has already run. So this does not work: ~~~text SELECT dept, name, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn FROM employees WHERE rn = 1; -- error: misuse of aliased window function rn ~~~ The fix is to compute the rank in one step and filter in the next, where rn is an ordinary column. ### Step pattern: top earner per department ~~~sql WITH ranked AS ( SELECT dept, name, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn FROM employees ) SELECT dept, name, salary FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY dept; ~~~ - WITH ranked AS (...): the first step. Every employee gets a number within their department. - PARTITION BY dept: restart the numbering for each department. - ORDER BY salary DESC: the highest salary gets number 1. - WHERE rn = 1: in the main query, rn is a plain column, so WHERE can use it. - ORDER BY dept: sort the final list. The result has 3 rows: Exec, Sofia Laurent (180000); Finance, Lea Fontaine (140000); Tech, Marc Durand (150000). ### The same pattern on products ~~~sql WITH ranked AS ( SELECT category, name, price, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC) AS rn FROM products ) SELECT category, name, price FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY category; ~~~ - The partition is now the category; the rank is by price. The result has 4 rows: Books, SQL Cookbook (45); Electronics, Laptop Pro 14 (1299); Furniture, Standing Desk (499); Grocery, Coffee Beans 1kg (18.9). ### Aggregate first, then rank Often the value to rank does not exist in a table yet: it has to be computed with joins and GROUP BY first. Chain two CTEs: the first aggregates, the second ranks. Here: each customer's biggest non-cancelled order. ~~~sql WITH order_totals AS ( SELECT o.customer_id, o.id AS order_id, SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS total FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY o.id ), ranked AS ( SELECT customer_id, order_id, total, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY total DESC) AS rn FROM order_totals ) SELECT c.name, r.order_id, ROUND(r.total, 2) AS total FROM ranked r JOIN customers c ON c.id = r.customer_id WHERE r.rn = 1 ORDER BY c.name; ~~~ - order_totals: joins three tables, skips cancelled orders in WHERE, and groups by order: one row per order with its total. It keeps customer_id so the next step can partition on it. - ranked: reads order_totals and numbers each customer's orders, biggest first. - The main query: keeps rn = 1, joins customers to show names, rounds only at the very end, and sorts. The result has 7 rows, one per customer with a non-cancelled order. Alice Martin's biggest is order 1 (1328.9) and Grace Lee's is order 9 (1548). David Kim does not appear: his only order was cancelled, so he has no row in order_totals. ### Dropping rows before ranking If some rows should not compete at all, remove them in the first step with WHERE. For example, with customers, WHERE c.city IS NOT NULL keeps people without a city out of every city's ranking. Filtering early is simpler than cleaning up afterwards, and remember that = NULL never works: use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. ### ROW_NUMBER or RANK? ROW_NUMBER always gives exactly one row number 1 per group, even if two rows tie; which one wins a tie is not guaranteed. RANK gives 1 to every tied row, so WHERE rnk = 1 could return two winners for one group. Choose ROW_NUMBER when the question asks for exactly one row per group. ### Common mistakes - Filtering on the window function in the same SELECT where it is computed. - Partitioning by the wrong column: the partition is the "per" in "per city" or "per department". - Ordering ascending inside OVER, so rank 1 is the smallest instead of the biggest. - Rounding before ranking or summing. Round once, in the final SELECT. - Forgetting the final ORDER BY when the question asks for a sorted list. ### Recap - To keep the top row per group: CTE with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY value DESC) AS rn, then WHERE rn = 1 outside. - When the value must be computed, add an earlier CTE with the joins, WHERE and GROUP BY. - Filter out unwanted rows (cancelled orders, NULL groups) in the first step. - Round and sort in the final SELECT.
